title: 2 Chronicles 10:16–19
context: When Rehoboam refuses to listen, the northern tribes reject David’s house with the cry, “Every man to your tents, Israel!” Rehoboam keeps only the Israelites living in the cities of Judah. He sends Hadoram, the overseer of forced labor, whom the people stone to death, and Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem. The parallel is 1 Kings 12:16–19, which names the overseer Adoram. Unlike 1 Kings 12:20, Chronicles does not narrate Jeroboam’s being made king over Israel; its focus stays on Judah and David’s house. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: the division is a real tragedy brought on by Rehoboam’s folly and the fulfillment of God’s word.

verses.text: When all Israel saw that the king didn’t listen to them, the people answered the king, saying, “What portion do we have in David? We don’t have an inheritance in the son of Jesse! Every man to your tents, Israel! Now see to your own house, David.” So all Israel departed to their tents.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel rejects David’s house: “What portion do we have in David?… Every man to your tents, Israel!” Arminian readers see the people responding to oppression with a choice of their own. The cry echoes Sheba’s rebellion in 2 Samuel 20:1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word through Ahijah coming to pass, even as the tribes act on their grievance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a real and tragic breach, noting both the people’s legitimate complaint and the sorrow of a divided people of God.

verses.text: But as for the children of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam reigns over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah. Arminian readers note that his kingdom is now greatly reduced as a consequence of his folly. Yet a remnant remains, and the line of David continues to rule in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the remaining kingdom God’s faithfulness to David, as promised (1 Kings 11:36). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing loss and preservation together: Rehoboam’s folly costs him much, but God keeps his promise of a lamp for David.

verses.text: Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was over the men subject to forced labor; and the children of Israel stoned him to death with stones. King Rehoboam hurried to get himself up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam sends Hadoram, the overseer of forced labor, and the people stone him; Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem. Arminian readers see poor judgment compounding his earlier folly. 1 Kings 12:18 names the overseer Adoram.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the choice of envoy as provocative and the violence as a sign of deep resentment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse plainly as the moment the breach becomes irreparable, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 12:18.

verses.text: So Israel rebelled against David’s house to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: “So Israel rebelled against David’s house to this day.” Arminian readers note the lasting consequences of choices made at Shechem. The division endured for generations, a sober reminder of how pride and harshness can do lasting harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the permanence of the division and see God’s word through Ahijah fulfilled. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summing up a real tragedy, in which both human responsibility and divine purpose are at work, and as setting the stage for Judah’s story.
